activities.caption: file each material by what its bands allow
activities.name: sdBandBuckets

config.prompt: One energy map, three conducting classes — file each material:

items.label: a half-filled highest band — electrons at the top drift freely
full valence band, no electron can be promoted — nothing conducts

config.why: Same bookkeeping everywhere: overlap → always conducting; about 1 eV → promotable by heat, light or impurity; 5+ eV → locked. The semiconductor is the tunable middle.

activities.caption: drag between the two resistors under the same warmth
activities.name: sdThermistorCompare

config.prompt: Two resistors, one heat source — drag between their responses:

before.label: the metal resistor
before.text: Conductivity falls as temperature rises: lattice vibrations scatter the electrons it already has. Warm it and resistance climbs.

after.label: the semiconductor resistor
after.text: Heat promotes carriers across the gap — the carrier population rises exponentially. Warm it and resistance drops.

config.why: The mechanisms are opposites, not merely different sizes — which is exactly what makes a thermistor possible.

activities.anchor: the effect is the lesson's showpiece
activities.caption: pair each dopant fact with its consequence
activities.name: sdDopantMatch

config.prompt: Substitutional doping, atom by atom — pair each move with what it buys:

pairs.right: four electrons complete the bonds; the fifth sits in a shallow donor level just under the conduction band
one bond left unsatisfied — an acceptor that steals an electron and leaves a mobile hole: p-type
doping also fixes the minority-carrier population — raising electrons suppresses holes
shifts toward whichever band the dopant feeds — the energy-space thermometer every device reads

config.why: One foreign atom in five million, near-perfect yield per atom — the arithmetic behind a factor of ~500,000 in conductivity.

activities.anchor: a barrier exactly as tall as the Fermi-level difference
activities.caption: rebuild how a boundary becomes a diode
activities.name: sdJunctionOrder

config.prompt: Join p to n and a device assembles itself — drag the steps into order:
items: Mobile carriers diffuse down their gradients — electrons into p, holes into n
Each crossing exposes the fixed dopant ions left behind
The exposed charge strip — the depletion region — builds an electric field
The field opposes further diffusion until equilibrium: a built-in barrier near 0.7 V for silicon
Forward bias lowers the barrier, and majority carriers flood across
config.why: Current then grows about tenfold per ~60 mV — the steepest useful switch curve in technology, all from immobile charges steering mobile ones.

activities.caption: call the photon energy behind a colour
activities.name: sdLedEstimate

config.prompt: Photon energy E ≈ 1240/λ(nm) eV. A green LED emits at 530 nm — roughly what photon energy does its gap need?
config.why: 1240/530 ≈ 2.3 eV (red at 650 nm needs ~1.9 eV; blue at 450 nm ~2.75 eV). Gap engineering is colour engineering — and the direct-gap III–V family supplies the palette.
config.context: Silicon can absorb fine (solar cells work) but cannot emit efficiently: an indirect gap needs a phonon to fix the momentum mismatch.

activities.anchor: keep the gate's field in charge of the channel
activities.caption: walk the switch-control decision
activities.name: sdGateBranch

config.root: You need a switch that flips billions of times per second at almost no control-energy cost.

start.text: Where does the control signal attach?

choices.label: A third terminal over a thin insulator — a MOSFET gate
choices.feedback: Control by field: the architecture that scales to billions.

choices.label: Inject a control current straight into the channel
choices.feedback: Control by current pays on every switch.

choices.label: Build the channel from gapless graphene
choices.feedback: Fast — but a conductor looking for a switch.

field.text: Gate voltage electrostatically inverts the channel surface and turns conduction on. The insulator blocks DC gate current, so switching costs only charging and discharging a tiny capacitance — which is what lets billions sit on one chip.

current.text: Every switch spends control energy, and the control wiring melts long before the transistors do. Moore's-law scaling — high-k dielectrics, strained silicon, FinFETs, gate-all-around — exists to keep the gate's field in charge instead.

graphene.text: Gapless means always conducting: there is no barrier for a gate to lower, no off-state to steer toward. MoS₂ and other 2-D materials with usable gaps wait at the research edge for exactly this reason.

config.why: The MOSFET is the junction given a steering terminal — the transistor's quiet miracle is control by field, not by current.

activities.anchor: like a valve handle under force
activities.caption: true or false — neutrality and the gate, audited
activities.name: sdNeutralJudge

statements.s: Doping fills the crystal with electrons the way a bucket fills, leaving it negatively charged overall.
statements.why: The crystal stays neutral: every fixed donor ion (+) is balanced by a mobile electron (−). What changes is which charges are mobile.

statements.s: A crystal doped to 10¹⁶ donors per cm³ still holds only a few carriers per million atoms.
statements.why: 10¹⁶ carriers against 5 × 10²² atoms — the effect is astronomical in conductivity and tiny in headcount.

statements.s: A MOSFET gate carries a steady control current while the switch is held open.
statements.why: The gate sits on an insulator — in steady state no DC gate current flows at all. It is a small capacitor.

statements.s: Switching a MOSFET costs only the energy to charge and discharge its gate capacitance.
statements.why: Control by field, not by current — the reason billions can switch on one chip without melting.

activities.anchor: why wafer maps read like epidemiology
activities.caption: one line of the morning-meeting note inverts the yield math
activities.name: sdYieldSpot

config.prompt: A fab's yield note — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: A 300 mm wafer hosts hundreds of dies.
A defect landing anywhere on a die kills that die.
If defects land at random, the fraction of good dies falls steeply as die area grows.
So doubling the die area roughly doubles the yield — monster dies are the profitable default.
Cleanrooms are graded like operating theatres, and "defects per cm²" opens the morning meeting.
config.correction: Double the area and yield collapses — a bigger die gives random defects more chances to land on it. Monster dies are reserved for products with monster prices.
config.why: Yield arithmetic is why fabs cost tens of billions: one defect per billion is the difference between a chip and a paperweight.
